ety.text: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).

senses.d: Placed separately (in regard to space or time).
ex: We had a large bus and I had two of them at the front and two at the back, and I had to sit in the middle and keep them apart.
Others apart sat on a hill retired.

senses.d: In or into two or more parts.
ex: We took the computer apart and put it back together.
Love, love will tear us apart, again.
Let Pleasure go, put Care apart.
Joking apart, what do you think?
In aristocracies, servants are a class apart.

senses.d: Having been taken apart; disassembled, in pieces.

grp.label: separately, in regard to space or company
in two or more parts; asunder

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin distantem (“being far”), present participle of distō (“to be far”). By surface analysis, distar + -ante.
Literally, “to pieces”.
From French appartement, from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”), equivalent to apart + -ment. See apart and -ment.

senses.d: A complete domicile occupying only part of a building, especially one for rent; a flat.
ex: I am Jonathan. I am in apartment B4. — I am in apartment C2.

senses.d: A suite of rooms within a domicile, designated for a specific person or persons and including a bedroom.
A division of an enclosure that is separate from others; a compartment.
A conceptual space used for separation in the threading architecture. Objects in one apartment cannot directly access those in another, but must use a proxy.

grp.label: domicile occupying part of a building
archaic: suite of rooms within a domicile

Inherited from Latin vivenda, feminine future participle of vīvō (“to live”). Compare Portuguese vivenda, Occitan vivenda; cf. also French viande (whence the Spanish doublet vianda was borrowed).

Borrowed from Italian appartamento, possibly through French appartement and/or Spanish apartamento. Ultimately from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”), from apartar (“to separate”). By surface analysis, apartar + -mento.

Middle French a partbor. Dutch apart Proto-Indo-European *keyt-der. Proto-Germanic *haiduzder. Proto-West Germanic *-haidu Old Dutch -heit Middle Dutch -heit Dutch -heid Dutch apartheid Afrikaans apartheidbor. English apartheid Borrowed from Afrikaans apartheid (literally “separateness, apartness”) (1929 in a South African socio-political context), from Afrikaans apart (“separate”) + suffix -heid, cognate of English -hood.

senses.d: The policy of racial segregation in South Africa from 1948 to 1994.
ex: She don't care about the rest at all / She's got a system they call apartheid / It keeps a brother in a subjection

senses.d: Any similar policy of racial segregation or separation and discrimination, particularly when in favor of a minority rule.
ex: The 1973 Apartheid Convention conferred universal jurisdiction to the state signatories to prosecute those who commit apartheid.
When the doors of a business are open to the public, they must be open to all regardless of race if apartheid is not to become engrained in our public […] .

senses.d: A policy or situation of segregation based on some specified attribute.
ex: In these annual reports, the religious apartheid practices in India are not mentioned at all.

senses.d: To impose a policy of segregation of groups of people, especially one based on race.
ex: Yes, apartheiding the apartheiders, is what the rest of the world is doing.
Whatever the reason the blacks have for "apartheiding" Boston, whites should be all for it.

grp.label: policy of racial separation in South Africa
any policy of racial separation — see also segregation
